nameStory: Lemon balm gets its delightful name from the fresh, citrusy scent that bursts forth when you crush its leaves between your fingers. The genus name Melissa comes from the ancient Greek word for 'honey bee' – a perfect tribute to this plant's amazing ability to attract these buzzing pollinators to your garden.
description: Lemon balm is a cheerful, bushy herb in the mint family that fills the air with a lovely lemon fragrance. This perennial plant grows up to about 3 feet tall, forming spreading clumps of bright green, heart-shaped leaves. In summer, it produces tiny white or pale pink flowers that bees absolutely adore. Originally from Europe and Asia, it now grows wild throughout New England and is a favorite in herb gardens.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves with toothed edges that release an unmistakable lemony scent when rubbed – like a cross between lemon and mint

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Square stems that are characteristic of the mint family, with leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white or very pale pink flowers clustered in small groups along the upper stems, blooming from summer into fall

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Leaves feel slightly fuzzy and soft to the touch, with a wrinkled, textured surface that holds the aromatic oils

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dark brown nutlets that form after flowering – the plant also spreads by underground runners

habitat: Lemon balm thrives in rich, moist soils and can be found in gardens, along roadsides, and in partially shaded areas throughout New England. It's commonly escaped from cultivation and naturalized in disturbed areas, forest edges, and anywhere the soil stays reasonably moist. You'll often find it growing alongside other herbs and weedy plants in semi-wild spaces.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as fresh, bright green shoots with that characteristic lemony scent already noticeable in young leaves.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with full, lush foliage and the appearance of small white or pale pink flower clusters that attract numerous bees and other pollinators.
seasonality.fall: Plants continue blooming into early fall, with leaves maintaining their fragrance until the first hard frost kills back the above-ground portions.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground, but the underground root system and runners remain alive, ready to send up new growth in spring.

funFact: Lemon balm has been used since at least the 16th century specifically to attract honey bees to gardens – medieval beekeepers would rub it on their hives to encourage bees to return home and attract new swarms!
confusionNotes: Lemon balm can be confused with other mints, but the distinctive lemony scent (not spearmint or peppermint) is the dead giveaway. Remember: if it smells like lemon when crushed and has heart-shaped leaves, you've found lemon balm!
contextualKnowledge: While called 'lemon balm,' this plant isn't related to actual lemon trees – it's purely a mint family member that happens to contain citrus-scented compounds. It's been used in traditional medicine and cooking for centuries, and you might find it listed in old herbals as 'bee balm,' though that name more commonly refers to the completely different Monarda species.
compareHints: Lemon balm is the only Melissa species commonly found in New England, making it unique in its genus here. Compared to other mints in the family, it's distinguished by its heart-shaped (rather than lance-shaped) leaves and lemony (rather than minty) scent. Unlike bee balm (Monarda), which has showy tubular flowers, lemon balm's flowers are tiny and inconspicuous.
